t: Maximum Size of a Set After Removals
o: Remove exactly n/2 elements from each of two arrays, then union the remainders into a set; maximize the set size. Distinct values appearing in only one array can each contribute one element from their array. Values common to both arrays contribute via whichever array has spare capacity. Plan: keep one copy of as many unique-to-array values as fit in n/2 slots, then fill remaining slots with common values. Examples check out: [1,2,3,4,5,6]/[2,3,2,3,2,3] → 3 uniques kept in nums1 + min(2 commons, 3 spare) = 5.
k: Each array retains exactly n/2 elements; only set membership matters, so keep at most one copy of each distinct value per array.
Unique-to-array values must come from their own array; common values can be covered by either.
Greedy: reserve slots for uniques first, spend leftovers on commons.

a.i: Let o1, o2 be counts of values unique to each array and c the common count. Keep k1 = min(o1, n/2) uniques in array 1, k2 in array 2; spare slots (n/2 − k1) + (n/2 − k2) can each cover one additional common value. Answer = k1 + k2 + min(c, spares).
s: Return k1 + k2 + min(c, n − k1 − k2)

a.i: Actually choose which elements to keep: one copy of each unique value (up to n/2), then pad with common values, then pad with duplicates; union the kept sets. Verifies the greedy concretely and handles interviewer pushback about feasibility of filling slots.
s: Pick uniques from nums1 up to n/2, pad with anything else

w: The formula version is what you should write under time pressure; the constructive version is your proof sketch. Pitfall: you must remove EXACTLY n/2 (padding with duplicates is always possible since arrays have n elements), and common values kept in BOTH arrays waste slots — the min(c, spares) term encodes sharing. Follow-up: what if removal counts differed per array?
